title: Design live streaming for IND vs PAK
dek: On 14 October 2023, 3.5 crore people watched India play Pakistan live on one streaming app, all at the same time. Design the service that sends them the match: the crowd arrives at the toss within minutes, the last over is the busiest moment, and a stall of a few seconds is seen by crores.

items: A CDN carries the match. No server farm takes 87.5 lakh requests a second; the edges answer 99 in 100 near the viewers, so your servers see 87,500.
Live is harder than recorded video: every 4-second segment is new, so the edges fetch it from your origin first, and an origin failure reaches every viewer within seconds.
The crowd arrives at the toss in minutes, faster than servers boot. Start the capacity before 7 pm, sized from past matches; keep autoscaling for surprises.
Plan to degrade, not to fall over: drop the highest quality, switch off the extras, keep the picture going.
Stream one match to every viewer as it happens, on phones, TVs and laptops, from the toss to the presentation.
Several qualities, from 240p to 1080p; the player picks one to suit its network and switches as the network changes.
Viewers are only a few seconds behind the real match, never minutes.
Show how many people are watching right now.
Out of scope: sign-up and payments, ads inserted into the stream, commentary in other languages, replays after the match.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: 3.5 crore watching at once at the peak
Stalls rare, even at the toss and in the last over; quality drops before the picture stops
About 10 to 30 seconds behind the stadium
The stream never stops for everyone at once

items: Viewers: 3.5 crore at the peak, in the last over at 10:18 pm (the real record, India v Pakistan, 14 October 2023, as reported by the broadcaster). At the 7 pm toss the audience jumps from about 10 lakh to 1.4 crore within 15 minutes.

Requests: a player fetches a 4-second segment every 4 seconds, so 3.5 crore players make 87.5 lakh requests a second. Playlists, refreshed as often, are a few hundred bytes and almost always answered at the edge.
Bandwidth: at about 1.5 Mbps each (most watch on phones, at 480p or 720p), 3.5 crore players pull about 50 Tbps. That is more than one CDN carries in India; big broadcasters split it across several.
Origin: if the edges answer 99 in 100, your servers see 87,500 requests a second at the peak. At 2,500 a second per server that is 35 servers flat out; plan for 40, in two groups.
Writes: one camera feed in 6 sizes makes 6 new segments and 6 updated playlists every 4 seconds. Writes are tiny; this is the most read-heavy system in the library.
Stream: `id` (ind-vs-pak), `status` (scheduled, live, ended), the qualities on offer.
Segment: `stream_id`, `quality`, `seq` (one every 4 seconds), the bytes. A file, written once and never changed.
Playlist: `stream_id`, `quality`, the newest few segment numbers. Rewritten every 4 seconds.
Viewer count: `stream_id`, an estimate updated every few seconds.

body.label: API
body.x:
GET /live/ind-vs-pak/master.m3u8          → the qualities on offer
GET /live/ind-vs-pak/720p/playlist.m3u8   → the newest segments in 720p (asked for every 4 s)
GET /live/ind-vs-pak/720p/1834.ts         → segment 1834: 4 seconds of the match
GET /live/ind-vs-pak/viewers              → { "watching": 35000000 }
body.say: A master playlist lists the qualities. Each quality's playlist lists its newest segments, and the player asks for it every 4 seconds. The player then fetches segments by number. One more call returns how many people are watching.

body.cap: The stadium feed is encoded into six sizes and cut into 4-second segments, which the packager writes to storage with the playlists. Players fetch both through CDN edges; only what an edge doesn't have yet reaches the origin servers.

body.x: Two flows of very different sizes. Getting video in is one feed and small: encoders and a packager, in two places, writing every segment to storage. Getting video out is everything: the CDN answers almost every request, and your origin servers answer only what the edges ask for, about once per edge per segment.

body.cap: Autoscaling adds servers after the load has arrived, and each takes minutes to start, so at the toss it is always behind and players buffer. Servers started before 7 pm are ready when the crowd is.

items: Autoscaling reacts to load that has already arrived, and a new server takes minutes to boot and warm up. At the toss that is too late: the first servers overload and crash, and their viewers pile onto the rest.

A match has a start time and a peak you can predict from past matches; India v Pakistan on a weekend night is the biggest of the year. Start the capacity an hour before, sized for that peak, and keep autoscaling only for surprises.
Tell the CDNs the expected traffic in advance, and rehearse at a fraction of the load a few days before, with the same players and the same playlists.
Sign-ins arrive in the same minutes. Keep them cheap: a signed token the edge can check, entitlements cached, no database read per viewer.
A recorded film's segments sit at the edge for days. A live segment is new every 4 seconds: each edge fetches it from the origin the first time a player asks for it.
So the origin must never stop. Run it in two groups, ideally in two regions, each able to carry most of the peak alone; one group failing must not take the stream with it.

Request collapsing: when 10,000 players at one edge ask for segment 1834 at once, the edge sends one request to the origin and answers them all from that copy. An origin shield, a middle layer of caches, does the same for all the edges in a region.
Playlists change every 4 seconds: let the edge keep one for a second or two, not more, or players fall behind the match.
Drop the highest quality first. Without 1080p, players step down to 720p, which the edges already hold; everyone keeps playing and the bandwidth falls by a third.
Switch off the extras: chat, emoji reactions, recommendations, the animated scorecard. They can wait; the picture can't.
Use two or more CDNs. If one struggles in a region, send new players to another, from the player or through DNS.
Run encoders and packagers in two places, both writing every segment. If one fails, the playlists keep pointing at the other's segments.

body.x: The number on screen is an estimate. The origin can't count viewers: it sees about 1 request in 100. Instead each player sends a small heartbeat every 30 seconds, or each edge reports how many players it served in the last minute, and a job adds up a few hundred numbers every few seconds and rounds to the nearest lakh. An exact count would mean crores of writes to one table for no gain; 'Counting the uncountable' in Concepts covers the sketches that make such counts cheap.

items: Junior / mid: a CDN in front, segments and playlists, servers behind it, and the 87.5 lakh a second sum.
Senior: why live is harder than recorded and what an origin failure means, request collapsing and an origin shield, adaptive quality, capacity started before the toss.
Lead: several CDNs and how to split traffic between them, degrading by quality and by feature, rehearsals and a capacity plan from past matches, the viewer count as an estimate.

"How far behind the stadium is the stream?" Encoding and packaging take a few seconds, and players keep about 3 segments buffered (12 seconds). Shorter segments, or low-latency HLS with parts of a second, bring it under 10 seconds at the cost of many more requests.
"Ads in the over breaks?" Insert them on the server side, as segments in the playlist, so every player behaves the same and ad blockers don't break playback.
"One region's internet link is congested?" Players there drop quality by themselves; route new players in that region to the CDN with room.
"Replays after the match?" The same segments, now unchanging, become a recorded video: see 'Design video streaming'.

practice.brief: Each test sends what 3.5 crore players ask for: a 4-second segment of the match every 4 seconds, following the match night (quiet all day, a jump at the 7 pm toss, a dip at the innings break and the peak in the last over at 10:18 pm, 87.5 lakh requests a second). A CDN answers 99 in 100 at the edge, but this is live: every new segment comes from your servers first, so their failures reach every viewer. What the CDN doesn't answer reaches your servers, which make one lookup each, mostly answered by a cache. Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

tests.name: The toss
tests.desc: 7 pm: the crowd arrives within minutes, from 3 lakh to 1.4 crore players by 7:15.

checks.label: No buffering around the toss (7:05 to 7:35 pm): 99.95% of requests work
The video goes out through a CDN

tests.name: The last over
tests.desc: 10 pm to 11 pm: the peak, 3.5 crore players at 10:18 pm, then everyone leaves within minutes.

checks.label: No buffering in the last over (10:10 to 10:35 pm): 99.95% of requests work

tests.name: The whole match
tests.desc: 7 pm to 11 pm, toss to presentation.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of requests work over the evening
Segments and playlists are kept in storage built for files

tests.name: An origin group dies
tests.desc: At 8:10 pm, in the first innings, the busiest group of origin servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of requests still work
No origin group that every viewer depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A day without a match: 20,000 people watching replays, 5,000 requests a second all day. Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

tests.name: Play the next segment
tests.desc: A player asks for segment 1834 of the match in 720p.

tests.name: What's new in the stream
tests.desc: Every 4 seconds a player asks for the 720p playlist, which lists the newest segments.

wrong.name: No CDN
wrong.why: Every player's request reaches your own load balancer and servers: 87.5 lakh a second at the peak, far past what any server farm takes.

wrong.name: Autoscaling from a few
wrong.why: Two groups that start with 3 servers each and grow with the load. The crowd arrives at the toss in minutes; new servers take 4 minutes to boot, and the first ones crash under the rush.

wrong.name: Just enough servers
wrong.why: 30 servers take 75,000 requests a second. The last over needs 87,500 at the origin: too few, and they crash at the peak.

wrong.name: One origin group
wrong.why: 40 servers in one group behind the load balancer. When it crashes, every new segment stops reaching the edge and all 1.7 crore viewers buffer.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Two groups of 50 servers, running all day: it survives every match, but pays for far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.

wrong.name: Segments in the database
wrong.why: Video segments are stored as rows in a relational database: huge rows, slow reads and a database bill instead of cheap file storage.

hints.x: One match, one camera feed, crores of people at the same moment. What do they all ask for, and how often?
3.5 crore players each fetch a 4-second segment every 4 seconds. Divide; then take the 1% the CDN can't answer.
A player reads a playlist that lists the newest segments, then fetches the segments themselves: two GETs on files.
No server farm takes 87.5 lakh requests a second. Put a CDN in front: it answers 99 in 100 near the viewers, so size your servers for the rest.
Size the origin for the last over: 1% of 87.5 lakh is 87,500 a second, and a c5.2xlarge takes 2,500. Leave room, and split the servers into two groups so one can fail.
Everyone arrives at the toss within minutes, faster than new servers boot (4 minutes). Start them all before 7 pm instead of autoscaling from a few.
Segments and playlists are files that change every 4 seconds: keep them in object storage, with a cache in front, not in database rows.

practice.referenceNote: The canvas counts requests, not bandwidth: at the peak the real stream is about 50 Tbps, carried by several CDNs. The encoders that turn the stadium feed into segments aren't drawn; every 4 seconds they write a new segment in each size to storage and update the playlists.

decisions.q: Everyone arrives within minutes of the 7 pm toss. How do you have enough origin servers?
options: Autoscale on load and let new servers catch up with the crowd
Start them all before 7 pm, sized for the expected peak
Watch the dashboards and add servers by hand as load grows
decisions.why: New servers take minutes to boot and warm up, and the crowd arrives faster than that, so autoscaling is always behind at the toss. A match has a known start time and a peak you can predict from past matches: start the capacity before it, and keep autoscaling only for surprises.

decisions.q: Why does an origin failure hurt more for live video than for a recorded film?
options: Live viewers watch in higher quality, so each failure costs more
Live video can't be cached at all, so the CDN plays no part
Each new segment must come from the origin before any edge has it
decisions.why: A recorded film's segments sit at the edge for days, so a broken origin goes unnoticed for popular videos. A live segment is new every 4 seconds: the edges fetch it from the origin first, so when the origin stops, every viewer runs out of video within seconds. The CDN still matters: it turns crores of requests for each segment into one per edge.

decisions.q: How do you show '3.5 crore watching' without slowing the stream?
options: Edges count their own players; a small job adds the counts up
Each player adds a row to one table when it starts and stops
The origin servers count the requests reaching them each second
decisions.why: Most requests never reach your origin (the edges answer them), so it can't count viewers, and a row per player is crores of writes to one table in a few minutes. Counts per edge, or from a sample of player heartbeats, add up to an estimate in seconds, and the screen only shows it to the nearest lakh.
